menu.label: a
menu.action: move to the nearest left target by circling around the stick clockwise

menu.label: b
menu.action: move to the nearest right target by circling around the stick clockwise

menu.label: c
menu.action: move to the nearest left target by circling around the stick counterclockwise

  remaining_path
      When memory is empty and demonstration frames are present, decode the entire demonstration in two stages. First construct a temporary traversal ledger from the demonstration alone, excluding the reset to the execution starting scene. Anchor the ledger at the initial demonstrated highlighted target and initial wrist position, before any arrival change. Identify that starting target and every chronological arrival through the final demonstration arrival, identifying sites by stable horizontal order rather than exact fluctuating coordinates. The first distinct arrival closes the first traversal from this initial scene; it does not begin the route. Each consecutive pair of distinct adjacent sites creates one ledger row, even if that pair or destination has appeared before. Complete this arrival ledger before classifying any traversal; never compress its repeated rows. The ledger is temporary reasoning at this decision, not an additional memory field. Use highlight changes together with wrist arrival and subsequent motion to resolve each reached site. Temporary double highlights must not erase an arrival boundary. Suppress only coordinate jitter and duplicate indications of the same arrival; preserve every return to a previously visited site, immediate reversal, and repeated crossing as a separate traversal. Do not combine traversals into a net excursion. Second classify each ledger row independently. For that crossing, identify its departure and destination target sites, representative resting wrist positions at those endpoints, and intermediate wrist samples belonging to that crossing. Write any positions as [y, x]. Compute destination target x minus departure target x to determine horizontal direction; do not use a local reversal in wrist x. Judge the arc using the substantial interior wrist excursion relative to the line joining that row's endpoint wrist positions, not a near-arrival sample that may belong to the next crossing. For endpoint wrist positions [y0, x0] and [y1, x1] and an interior wrist sample [ys, xs], when x1 differs from x0, baseline_y = y0 + (y1 - y0) * (xs - x0) / (x1 - x0). Negative ys minus baseline_y indicates upper; positive indicates lower. Use wrist coordinates throughout this baseline calculation. Reversing horizontal direction does not by itself change the side of the baseline occupied by the arc. Use this table: larger x plus upper arc = A; larger x plus lower arc = C; smaller x plus upper arc = D; smaller x plus lower arc = B. Larger x is robot-left and smaller x is robot-right. Do not infer an arc from the preceding traversal, the net excursion, or a waypoint. Do not confuse the wrist with the attached stick endpoint or compare wrist height directly with target coordinates to classify the arc. Write exactly one letter per ledger row in chronological order. Verify a one-to-one correspondence between rows and letters, retaining every repeated crossing and the row ending at the final demonstration arrival. Explicitly check that the first row covers the motion from the demonstration's initial scene to its first distinct arrival, and that its independently classified letter is the first entry of the list.
